```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(tidyverse)
library(ordinal)
library(broom)
library(mgcv)
```

```{r}
data <- read.csv('../../data/processed/q1/q1-analysis.csv') %>% as_tibble()
```

```{r}
head(data)
```

# Model 1: Ordinal Logistic Regression Model (assumes strict linear relationship)

```{r}
model_data <- data %>%
  select(n_ud_pstat, stat_comfort) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(
    # Treat comfort as an ordered categorical outcome
    stat_comfort = ordered(
      stat_comfort,
      levels = 1:5
    )
  )
glimpse(model_data)

```

```{r}
table(model_data$stat_comfort)

```

```{r}
table(model_data$n_ud_pstat)
```

```{r}
ordinal_fit <- clm(
  stat_comfort ~ n_ud_pstat,
  data = model_data,
  link = "logit"
)
```

```{r}
summary(ordinal_fit)

```
Interpretation: 
Large P-value assumes that there is not a stastically significant relationship between the two variables. 

# Model 2: GAM (Assumes flexible, non-linear relationship)

```{r}
model_data$stat_comfort_int <- as.integer(as.character(model_data$stat_comfort))

# Fit the ordinal GAM
gam_fit <- gam(
  stat_comfort_int ~ s(n_ud_pstat, k = 3), 
  family = ocat(R = 5), 
  data = model_data
)

summary(gam_fit)
```
Interpretation: 
Large F-value assumes that there is not a stastically significant relationship between the two variables. Because the GAM model is more flexible, it is doing a better job at fitting the data compared to the first model, but the result is still not statistically significant. The model explains 5.64% of the deviance. 

# Correlation Matrix

```{r}
cor.test(model_data$n_ud_pstat, as.numeric(model_data$stat_comfort), method = "spearman")
```
With a correlation coefficient close to zero and a high p-value, the Spearman test shows little to no relationship between the two variables.
